steps.text: Whisk the flour, baking powder, salt, and pepper together in a bowl. Whisk together the egg and milk in a separate bowl; stir in the flour mixture until a smooth dough is formed.

Fill a large pot with lightly salted water and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Once the water is boiling, cut the dough into bite sized pieces with scissors into the boiling water. Boil for 20 minutes; drain well.
Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-low heat; add the knefla and potatoes. Stirring occasionally, cook until the potatoes are tender and the knefla are golden brown, about 20 minutes.

review.reviewBody: It was refreshing to see a knefla recipe that isn't the popular soup. This is how I remember my German Russian grandmother making it. A few things: I would start with 1 1/4 cup flour and add more as needed. I thought this called for a lot of flour and I had to add extra liquid to the dough as it turned out crumbly. Like my grandmother, I par-boiled the potatoes in ham broth, removed the potatoes then cooked the knefla in the broth as well. Instead of frying in oil, I heated the butter until good and brown (med-high heat)and then fried the potatoes and knepfla. Also, I can't resist adding the toasted bread crumbs to this dish. I hadn't made this in years and came across this recipe by accident. Jogged my memory. Thanks. By the way, I grew up in SD, 100 miles or so west of Hoven, SD.

I taught school in Ellendale, ND, for 5 years back in the early 1980s. This recipe is as close as any to the way the ladies in our church made knepfla. In addition to parboiling the potatoes and frying in butter rather than oil, knepfla always included chopped onions in with the noodles and potatoes. At the last minute, a couple slices of bread, crumbled into random, medium-sized pieces, were tossed into the browning ingredients. Parsley, fresh or dried, or dill weed (fresh is best!) were added as garnish. As most ethnic traditional dishes, each woman has/had her own way of making and serving, but the variations were never far from the basic recipe. This dish is hearty farm food, made with love and ingenuity from a pantry far different from today's. Those living on the prairies of Russia or the US often had little more than flour, potatoes, salt, and ingredients from their own chickens and a cow. What creativity!

I love that you're highlighting an old German recipe which was a staple in my family and that I still make today but the only difference I see is that the potatoes are usually boiled till almost done before the dough pieces are added and cooked till they rise to the top. Drain liquid and add bread crumbs that have been browned in butter. Then eat it as is and fry left overs.

This is so awesome. We still make a version from Lyman SD that adds crushed bacon (a whole package) and an onion fried in the bacon grease. Other changes to this recipe: 5 cups flour, 6 eggs, and not as many potatoes, although I may add more next time!

Glad to see this recipe, my mother made this regularly but she made a stew first with beef, onion and potatoes, then added the dough. I thought the recipe was lost until I saw it here, so happy. One of my favorite dishes

This is my go to comfort dish. I eat this 2-3 times a month. Leftovers taste even better the next day! A few notes: I end up having to use about 1/2 cup of milk to get the dough the right consistency. I also knead it, roll it out and cut into bit size pieces. I like to add 1 diced onion to the potatoes when frying and I fry up the dough separately then mix together with the potatoes. Also, you are going to need to salt this dish to taste otherwise it is virtually flavorless.

Like someone else said, I lost my recipe somewhere as well. I remember most of it by heart but it has been a long time since I have made it. My grandmother on my mom's side came over from Germany and they lived in South Dakoto then came out to Oregon. She taught my mom how to make it and my mom showed my sister and me how to make it. Some of the main differences were that they didn't use milk but just water to make the dough. We also used chicken broth to boil it in and would add the dough to the broth and then put the cut up potatoes in and keep boiling it until the potatoes are done then drain it. Add freshly fried bread and enjoy. The next day if their are any leftovers we would put them in a pan and fry them adding two or three eggs and they were just as good if not a little better than the first night. I do like this recipe since they do that right away. Next time I will try it with the milk and egg to make the dough and try them. Of course we always had it with Kielbasa that was cooked in Sauerkraut. Thanks for the recipe and I look forward to trying it this way next time.

I grew up with this recipe! A couple of tips:

1) Don't ever mistake the baking powder for baking soda...the dough turns green (true story!)
2) don't put too many pieces into the water at once; they won't cook thoroughly and you'll have a runny mess.

Thanks for the great recipe!
Check out some of the comments with add ins...all great suggestions. We also serve and then pass the salt, as they can be a little bland when serve with no meat. LOVE to see this recipe on-line.
Mom would fry bread crumbs and stick in with the knefla's when they were done.

So excited I found this recipe. My Husband's grandmother taught me how to make this and I wrote it down step by step on an index card while we made it. The index card vanished from the drawer in my kitchen, along with all the others I had. This is exactly the way I remember her making it.
I love that I now see the recipe for this! I grew up having this version, not the soup. My goal is to reproduce the taste, smell, and texture that I remember from my childhood long ago. Thank you!

I haven't made this in years, I add cut ribeye to mine, topped with sour cream, Yummy I never knew the name. 
Thank you

This recipe was a lot of work and made a lot of dirty dishes. The flavor was ok considering how much effort it took. I served it with sausages and I would have to say that was the best part of the meal.
I love Russian food, but this recipe i am sorry to say my family did not like. I thought the instructions and ingredience sounded good, but the taste was not good. Thanks but no thanks
We added ours to our potato and chicken/cream then add vinegar to taste. Family loves these.

My sister Sandy and I were searching for Kuchen recipes and found this site. We were so excited to see this recipe as it brought back many happy memories at Grandma's table. We are orginally from a little town called Canova, SD which is near Salem. Thanks so much for sharing and what a coincidence that we live in PA as well.
